newsitem.title: USA: Judge orders DNA tests in British nanny murder trial.
newsitem.headline: Judge orders DNA tests in British nanny murder trial.

text.p: A judge on Monday ordered DNA tests done on the blood and skin of a 9-month-old baby allegedly killed by a British au pair who was taking care of him.

The DNA tests came at the request of lawyers for Louise Woodward, 19, of Chester, England, who is accused of murdering the infant, Matthew Eappen, in February. She remains in custody where she has been held since her Feb. 5 arrest.

Her lawyer, Andrew Good, asked for and got a month's delay to do DNA testing on blood and tissue samples of Eappen. He wamts to know if the infant had either of two genetic disorders that may cause bleeding inside the skull.
Good told Massachusetts Superior Court Judge Hiller Zobel his case did not rest solely on the results of the tests.
"Our case does not depend on the outcome of the tests. We would have defence even if the tests prove negative," Good argued.

In a written motion, Good said he wanted to determine whether Eappen suffered from either osteogenesis imperfecta or glutaric acidemia type one. The latter "makes a person particularly vulnerable to intracranial bleeding," according to the motion.
Eappen died from head injuries the equivalent prosecutors said earlier of being dropped from a second floor window.
Good then volunteered Woodward had passed a polygraph test and offered to have his client submit to a similar test for the prosecution, an offer prosecutor Lynn Rooney accepted.
Lie detector tests can be submitted as evidence only with the approval of prosecutors in Massachusetts and Judge Zobel ordered a July hearing on their admissibility.
He also granted a delay in the trial's start until Aug. 11 so that results in all the tests could be available. The trial had been scheduled to start July 14.
